title: From Rs 37,000 a Month to Rs 2.2 Crore: Indian Techie's Career Leap Without Elite Credentials
excerpt: A software engineer from a tier-3 college shares how strategic job switches, DSA mastery, and FAANG experience transformed his earning trajectory over eight years.
body:
• An Indian software engineer grew his salary from Rs 37,000 per month (Rs 4.7 LPA) to over Rs 2.2 crore annually in eight years, without an IIT, IIM, or tier-1 college degree.
  • The key strategy involved frequent job switches every 12-18 months early in his career, combined with intensive preparation in data structures and algorithms.
  • He progressed from a service-based startup to FAANG companies and eventually landed a Staff Engineer role at a multinational corporation.
  • His story has gone viral on social media, sparking debate about whether elite credentials are necessary for high-paying tech careers in India.

An Indian software engineer's journey from earning Rs 37,000 a month at a service-based startup to commanding an annual package exceeding Rs 2.2 crore has gone viral, offering a counterpoint to the widely held belief that only graduates of elite institutions can reach the top of India's tech salary ladder.

The engineer, who shared his story on social media and was profiled by NDTV and other outlets, graduated from a tier-3 college with a non-computer science degree. He had no IIT, IIM, or tier-1 credentials — the pedigree that many in India's tech industry consider a prerequisite for high-paying roles.

Building Skills From the Ground Up

His career began with freelancing during college, where he completed over 100 small projects using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP, and Node.js. That hands-on experience landed him his first full-time role at a service-based startup with a salary of Rs 4.7 lakh per annum — roughly Rs 37,000 per month after taxes.

Within 18 months, he switched to a product-based startup that tripled his salary. The workplace culture was imperfect, but the move exposed him to more complex engineering problems and set the stage for his next leap.

The FAANG Breakthrough

By his third year, he had invested heavily in mastering data structures and algorithms — the gateway to technical interviews at top global firms. The preparation paid off when he secured a role at a FAANG company with a compensation package of Rs 26 LPA, more than five times his starting salary.

At FAANG, he worked on distributed systems and complex infrastructure projects, eventually earning a promotion to SDE-II. A subsequent move to another FAANG company pushed his package to Rs 45 LPA.

Staff Engineer at Rs 2.2 Crore

After four years across two FAANG companies, he made what he described as his biggest career move — joining a multinational corporation as a Staff Engineer with an annual package exceeding Rs 2.2 crore. The jump represented a nearly 50x increase from his starting salary.

"No IIT, IIM or Tier 1 college. How this techie went from Rs 37k to Rs 2.2 crore."

— NDTV headline on the viral story

The story has resonated widely on platforms like Reddit and LinkedIn, where it has sparked debate about whether India's tech hiring obsession with institutional pedigree is outdated. Several commenters noted that while the trajectory is impressive, it required relentless upskilling, strategic timing, and tolerance for workplace instability during early career switches.

Lessons for Aspiring Engineers

The engineer's approach offers several takeaways for Indian tech professionals seeking similar growth. Early-career job switches every 12-18 months can yield salary jumps of 50-100%, far outpacing annual increments. Mastering DSA remains the single most effective lever for clearing interviews at top-tier companies. And real-world project experience — not credentials — is what ultimately distinguishes candidates in technical evaluations.

His story also underscores a broader trend: India's tech salary ceiling has risen dramatically for those with the right skills, even as entry-level salaries at major IT firms have barely moved in 15 years, with companies like TCS and HCL still offering Rs 3.5 LPA to fresh graduates.
nri_angle: The story resonates with Indian tech professionals both in India and abroad, highlighting how skills-based career growth can bypass the traditional credentialism of India's engineering education system.
author: Diaspora Desk
